content: The evaluation of evidence quality in research is categorized into four levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. A high grade signifies strong confidence that the evidence accurately reflects the true effect, with minimal likelihood that further research will alter this confidence. A moderate grade indicates reasonable confidence in the evidence, though additional research may influence the estimate. A low grade reflects limited confidence, suggesting that further studies are likely to change the estimate and potentially increase confidence. A very low grade implies that the evidence is either unavailable or too limited to draw conclusions due to significant study limitations, inconsistencies, imprecision, or reporting bias. Study Identification and Inclusion A total of 4,492 studies or abstracts were screened, including duplicates, from various sources such as PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, conference abstracts, and the WHO Global Hepatitis Programme’s network. Of these, 2,052 studies were from the main database search, 1,775 from EASL 2020, 558 from INHSU (2016–2019), 63 from IVHEM 2020, and 45 from the WHO network. After full-text screening of 119 studies from the main search, 12 were included. Additionally, nine studies from EASL 2020, five from INHSU, and 19 from the WHO network were included, resulting in a total of 45 studies. The geographic distribution and key features of these studies are summarized in supplementary materials. Study Characteristics Among the 45 included studies, 28 focused on people who inject drugs or homeless individuals, four on prisoners, nine on general or mixed populations, and four on people living with HIV. Nearly half (47%) of the studies were conducted in lowand middle-income countries, particularly among general or mixed populations and people living with HIV, but none among prisoners. All studies were observational, with 37 being prospective and eight retrospective; no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified. Risk of bias was high in 16 studies (36%), moderate in 18 (40%), and low in 11 (24%). The studies included 64 within-study arms, comprising 42 studies using point-of-care (PoC) RNA assays (45 arms) and 16 studies using lab-based assays (19 arms). PoC RNA assays were predominantly conducted on-site or in mobile units, while lab-based assays were used as comparators. The weighted RNA prevalence among those undergoing HCV antibody testing was 16%, with the highest prevalence observed in people who inject drugs and homeless individuals (27%), followed by people living with HIV (10%), general or mixed populations (6%), and prisoners (5%). Models of Care and Turnaround Times The studies employed various models of care for HCV testing and treatment. Among the 39 arms using on-site PoC RNA assays, five provided testing and treatment at the same site and visit, 23 at the same site but on different visits, and 11 at different sites and visits. For mobile PoC RNA assays, one arm conducted testing and treatment at the same site and visit, two at the same site but different visits, one at different sites on the same visit, and two at different sites and visits. Lab-based PoC RNA assays were used in six arms, with testing and treatment at the same site but different visits in four arms and at different sites and visits in two arms. Non-PoC lab-based RNA testing was used in 13 arms, with nine conducting testing and treatment at the same site but different visits and four at different sites and visits. The median time from HCV antibody testing to treatment initiation varied significantly across models of care. PoC RNA assays had the shortest pooled times, with on-site PoC assays averaging 13 days and mobile units achieving a median of 0 days. Lab-based testing had longer turnaround times, with lab-based PoC assays averaging 62 days and high-throughput lab-based assays averaging 43 days. Most delays occurred between RNA testing and treatment initiation. Uptake of RNA Testing and Treatment The uptake of RNA testing and treatment varied by model of care. For on-site PoC RNA assays, 95% of participants received RNA testing, compared to 84% for mobile PoC assays, 92% for lab-based PoC assays, and 82% for high-throughput lab-based assays. Treatment initiation rates were 77% for on-site PoC assays, 81% for mobile PoC assays, 89% for lab-based PoC assays, and 53% for high-throughput lab-based assays. Differences in uptake were influenced by the location and timing of testing and treatment delivery. Population Subgroups Among people who inject drugs and homeless individuals, RNA testing uptake was highest for on-site PoC assays (93%) and mobile units (84%), compared to lab-based assays (27%). Treatment uptake was also higher for PoC assays (73–81%) than for lab-based assays (59%). For prisoners, PoC assays demonstrated higher treatment uptake than lab-based assays, though RNA testing uptake was similar. Among people living with HIV, no high-throughput lab-based assays were available, but treatment uptake was higher for on-site PoC assays (75%) than for lab-based PoC assays (53%). Cost-Effectiveness Four studies included cost-effectiveness analyses. For example, a study in an English prison found that a simplified model of care using PoC RNA testing was cost-effective, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios well below the national willingness-to-pay threshold. Similarly, a study in Cambodia demonstrated cost savings with a simplified model of care, reducing the number of visits before treatment initiation from nine to three. However, the specific contribution of PoC RNA assays to cost-effectiveness could not be isolated in some studies. Conclusion Overall, PoC RNA assays, particularly those conducted on-site or in mobile units, demonstrated shorter turnaround times and higher uptake of RNA testing and treatment compared to lab-based assays. These findings highlight the potential of PoC assays to improve HCV care, especially among vulnerable populations such as people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, and prisoners. However, further research is needed to address gaps in evidence, particularly for certain population subgroups and cost-effectiveness analyses.
